title: Conjecture 1.1
statement_text: A graph is strongly perfect if and only if it contains no odd holes, no antiholes of length at least six, and none of the Graphs I, II, III, IV, V shown in Figure 1.
context_text: The conjecture, attributed to reference [8] and presented in 1990, proposes a forbidden induced subgraph characterisation of strongly perfect graphs via five infinite families. Graph VI (proposed by Maffray, appearing in Ravindra [9] in 1999) is an additional minimal non-strongly-perfect graph already showing the list is incomplete. The general characterisation of strongly perfect graphs remains open.
paper_contribution: Provides several new infinite families of minimal non-strongly-perfect graphs (emanations and mutations of Graphs II–VI) that are not among Graphs I–V of the conjecture, demonstrating that the forbidden induced subgraph list in Conjecture 1.1 is incomplete.

title: Informal Conjecture (outerplanar strongly perfect graphs)
statement_text: While obtaining a complete list of minimal non-strongly-perfect graphs appears to be out of reach, one might conjecture that the characterization of outerplanar strongly perfect graphs can be obtained through the minimal examples given in this paper.
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple. A strong stable set of $G$ is a stable set meeting every nonempty maximal clique of $G$. $G$ is strongly perfect if every induced subgraph has a strong stable set (a subclass of perfect graphs), and minimal non-strongly-perfect if it is not strongly perfect but all its proper induced subgraphs are. Characterizing strongly perfect graphs by forbidden induced subgraphs is open in general; the claw-free case was conjectured by Ravindra and proved by Wang. Ravindra also conjectured in 1990 that a graph is strongly perfect iff it contains no odd hole, no antihole of length at least six, and none of five specific graphs. Maffray later gave another minimal non-strongly-perfect graph. The present paper extends this list with several new infinite families of minimal non-strongly-perfect graphs. They are built from a larva (an even hole plus a vertex adjacent to two consecutive hole vertices) and its relatives, pupas and butterflies, by joining two such pieces by odd or even paths, by 'evolution' (subdividing a side edge an even number of times and making a hole vertex complete to the new vertices) and by 'mutation'. The minimal examples referred to in the statement are these families and the earlier known graphs, given in the paper by figures. The informal conjecture is that, restricted to outerplanar graphs, these examples suffice to characterize strong perfection, even though a complete list of all minimal non-strongly-perfect graphs seems out of reach.
